title: Zach Hopton
text:
I’m a PhD student at the University of Zurich, supervised by Eleanor Chodroff.
    As part of the SNF project “Strengthening the Role of Generative Machine Learning in Psycholinguistics,” I also work closely with Ryan Cotterell and his lab at ETH Zurich. My entry point to linguistics was amazement at how diverse the world’s languages are, and now my research reflects that with three major questions:
  
  


What are the underlying cognitive mechanisms that allow humans to use such a diverse range of languages efficiently?
What can speech processing models tell us about how sound patterns are realized across speakers and languages?
How can language technology be made to perform better for diverse language varieties?

To that end, my research usually falls somewhere in:

(Computational) Phonetics
(Computational) Psycholinguistics
Multilingual Speech and Language Technology

I also love to keep up with work on typology and hope to veer into the field more myself at some point.
More on the research page, or see my publications and CV (being updated).
In my free time, I enjoy all things cardio (running, cross-country skiing, and recently cycling), baking, and learning languages (predictable, I know). I particularly like mixing my running with travel, feel free to follow along on Strava!

title: Research
text:
In psycholinguistics research, surprisal is almost always computed from text, even in studies where people are listening to spoken input. We develop a framework to estimate it directly from the audio with speech language models. Doing so raises questions about units: one word has many acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by a given speech LM. Using importance sampling, we marginalize over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model and study this estimated marginalized surprisal as a predictor of pupil dilation in listening studies.
Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal (to appear at EMNLP 2026).

title: Research
text:
Getting the predictors right
Reading-time studies usually take contextual surprisal from a language model and word frequency from a separate corpus. We show how to estimate both from the same model. We test whether downstream models of eye-tracking data in 11 languages change when unigram and contextual surprisal come from the same model.

Explore the unigram surprisal results
Every model comparison from Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics (to appear at EMNLP 2026), across eleven MECO languages and three English corpora. Switch estimators, spillover, outlier removal, log-transformed reading times and multiple-comparison correction.

title: Research
section: Speech and text technology for language varieties
text:
Speech and text technology for language varieties
Dialect robustness in Catalan speech recognition, parallel data and a lemmatizer for the written varieties of Romansh, orthographic variation in Occitan, and low-resource speech translation. See publications.
